title: Malaysia prepares AI safety institute and enforcement plan ahead of its AI bill
excerpt: Malaysia's digital ministry says enforcement, AI safety testing and national AI standards are being prepared so a risk-based AI law can apply from day one.

sources.title: Bernama: AI Governance Bill To Supplement Existing Sectoral Laws -- Ministry of Digital
The Star: AI safety, enforcement framework prepped ahead of new Bill

body_html:
Malaysia's Ministry of Digital says it is preparing an enforcement framework, a national AI safety institute and AI standards so that the country's planned AI Governance Bill can be applied as soon as it becomes law. The bill is expected to be tabled in Parliament early next year.

The plans were set out on 17 November 2026 by Deputy Digital Minister Wilson Ugak Kumbong in a keynote at the Smart Nation Expo in Kuala Lumpur, according to Bernama, Malaysia's national news agency, and the newspaper The Star.

What is being prepared

According to both reports, the ministry described the bill as risk-based: the stricter rules would apply to AI uses that carry more risk. It would add to existing laws for individual sectors, such as finance or health, rather than replace them.

The ministry's lead agency for AI, AI Malaysia, is building:

  • an enforcement framework, so that rules can be enforced from the day the law takes effect;
  • a Malaysia AI Safety Institute, intended to carry out safety benchmarking and risk assessment and to handle incident or risk reporting;
  • national AI standards, known as MY-AI Standards, which are being developed with SIRIM, Malaysia's national standards and industrial research organisation.

The deputy minister also said that powerful autonomous systems would need testing, monitoring and human oversight before their use is expanded. The Star quoted him: "Whatever AI can suggest, people must always remain the ones who decide."

What is not yet known

The text of the AI Governance Bill has not been published. The reports do not give an exact tabling date, the penalties the bill would set, or which AI uses would count as higher risk. It is also not yet clear when the AI Safety Institute will start work, or how incident reports would be made and by whom. The early-2027 timing for the bill had been announced before; what is new is the detail on enforcement, safety testing and standards.

Why it matters for people staying in charge

Malaysia's plan to have enforcement ready from day one addresses a common gap: a law that exists on paper before anyone can check whether it is followed.

The ministry's emphasis on human oversight for autonomous systems matches D1 Always stoppable and D2 Bounded autonomy in the Humasure Directives: people decide how far a system may act on its own, and can stop it. Safety testing and incident reporting relate to D9 Accountable, which asks that someone answers when an AI system causes harm.

Whatever the final law says, anyone buying or using an AI product can ask its maker how it was tested and who to contact when something goes wrong. See Humasure's questions to ask.
